summary: Asks IANA to create a registry for fields in the IGMP message header and gives guidance for assigning values. It is a Best Current Practice. It was replaced by RFC 9778.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3228 asks IANA to maintain a registry for the Type and Code fields in the IPv4 IGMP header. It sets assignment procedures and reserves a range of code values for experiments.

subtitle: IANA assignment rules for fields in the IPv4 IGMP header.

tldr.problem: IGMP header Type and Code values need assignment rules and a central registry.
tldr.mechanism: Type values use IESG Approval or Standards Action; policies for codes are defined for each type. Code values 240 through 255 are reserved for testing and experimentation.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3228 is a Best Current Practice and was obsoleted by RFC 9778.

today: RFC 3228 is a Best Current Practice and was obsoleted by RFC 9778, according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: IGMP Type and Code Fields
sections.content: The IPv4 Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) header contains Type and Code fields whose values come from IANA-managed name spaces. Code values are defined relative to a specific Type. RFC 3228 requests a registry for these header fields and gives IANA guidance for assigning their values.
sections.plainLanguage: IGMP messages carry a Type and a related Code. This RFC gives IANA rules for keeping track of those values.

sections.title: Assignment and Experimental Values
sections.content: IGMP Type values are allocated through IESG Approval or Standards Action. Existing Type Code values use those procedures as well; a document defining a new Type should set the policy for its Code values. Code values 240 through 255, or 0xf0 through 0xff, are reserved for protocol testing and experimentation. Systems should silently ignore IGMP messages with unknown Code values.
sections.plainLanguage: New Types require IESG approval or a standards action. Code values 240 through 255 are set aside for experiments, and unknown Codes should be ignored.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC warns that firewalls and intrusion detection systems rely on clear interpretations of IGMP fields. If a tool does not understand a newly assigned value, it may block traffic or pass traffic without recognizing that the value could be used in an attack. The RFC says high visibility for assignments is important.
sections.plainLanguage: Security tools may not understand new values. Clear, visible assignment procedures help those tools account for changes.
